title: Self-Portrait

artist.name: Vincent van Gogh
artist.bioShort: Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose intense color, expressive brushwork, and emotional directness transformed modern art.
artist.bioLong: Vincent van Gogh developed his mature style during a short but astonishingly productive career. In Paris he absorbed Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist color, then transformed those lessons into a highly personal language of directional brushwork, complementary color, and psychological force.

texts.historicalContext: This 1889 self-portrait, now held by the Musée d’Orsay in Paris, belongs to the final phase of Van Gogh’s self-portraiture. Rather than presenting a social identity, the painting concentrates on self-examination through colour, brushwork, and the tension between a still pose and an intensely animated surface.
texts.artistBiography: Van Gogh used self-portraits as a practical and psychological laboratory. Unable to afford models consistently, he painted himself repeatedly, studying expression, color, identity, and the physical energy of brushwork.
texts.artisticAnalysis: Van Gogh places his head and upper body against a field of pale turquoise and green. The orange beard and hair act as complementary counterpoints, while the face remains comparatively still against the undulating strokes of the background. The suit gives the figure a formal stability that heightens the psychological intensity of the gaze.
texts.symbolism: The self-portrait becomes an act of scrutiny rather than simple likeness. The direct gaze, controlled posture, and turbulent surrounding strokes create a contrast between outward composure and inner intensity.
texts.composition: The bust-length figure is turned in three-quarter view. The face forms the visual anchor, while the background’s curved strokes echo the hair and beard and generate a continuous rhythm around the head.
texts.palette: Pale turquoise, absinthe green, blue-green, ochre, and orange dominate. The complementary opposition between the cool background and the fiery hair and beard creates the painting’s chromatic vibration.
texts.perspectiveTechnique: Van Gogh models the face with directional brushwork rather than smooth academic shading. Curved and rhythmic strokes in the background amplify movement around the relatively fixed head and torso.
texts.culturalSignificance: Van Gogh's self-portraits became icons of modern artistic identity, linking visible brushwork with interior feeling and turning the artist's face into a record of perception itself.
texts.influence: The work anticipates Expressionism and later modern portraiture by making color, touch, and psychological intensity as important as likeness.
interestingFacts: The Musée d’Orsay dates the work to 1889 and records its dimensions as 65 × 54.2 cm.
The painting is held by the Musée d’Orsay in Paris.
The Musée d’Orsay notes that Van Gogh produced more than 43 painted or drawn self-portraits over roughly ten years.
The cool green-turquoise background is set against the complementary orange of the hair and beard.

hotspots.label: Direct Gaze
hotspots.body: The eyes create a tense direct encounter with the viewer, turning the self-portrait into an act of observation and self-observation.

hotspots.label: Complementary Color
hotspots.body: The orange-red beard vibrates against the blue-green background, using complementary contrast to intensify the portrait.

hotspots.label: Broken Brushwork
hotspots.body: The background is not passive; its short marks create movement and emotional pressure around the figure.

hotspots.label: Dark Structure
hotspots.body: The dark jacket stabilizes the lower part of the image while repeating the same broken, directional brushwork seen in the face and background.
